newsitem.title: USA: Majority of Americans say tax cuts "unfair".
newsitem.headline: Majority of Americans say tax cuts "unfair".

text.p: Tax cuts in the budget agreement passed by Congress Thursday are "unfair" because they mostly benefit the rich, according to 58 percent of Americans surveyed by Time Magazine and CNN.
The results of the survey, released Saturday, showed only 27 percent viewed the cuts as "fair" to all Americans.
Few believe the agreement will benefit them personally, with only 29 percent seeing personal gains compared with 58 percent who did not consider they would benefit.
A majority of Americans doubt the claims by Congress and the White House that the new tax deal will produce a balanced budget by 2002.
The CNN/Time poll showed only 40 percent thought it "very or somewhat likely" that the deal would result in a balanced budget against 62 percent who said it was "somewhat or very unlikely."
After months of tough negotiations and heated rhetoric, Congress overwhelmingly approved legislation Thursday on a five-year spending and tax pact supposed to balance the budget by 2002.
The legislation, still to be signed by President Clinton, would provide a $500-per-child credit, cut the capital gains rate and provide breaks for higher education.
It also reduces Medicare by about $115 billion over five years, largely by cutting payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers.

Americans with more money were more in favour of the agreement. Though 61 percent favours the agreement (24 percent are opposed), more of those who earn $50,000-plus are in favour (65 percent) than those who earn under $20,000 (55 percent).

More Americans believe Clinton and the Republicans proposed the tax cuts to win political advantage (67 percent) than because they are good for the country (24 percent). More Americans gave the Republicans credit for completing the agreement (41 percent) than the president (32 percent).
The Time/CNN poll conducted on July 30-31, surveyed 814 people by phone. The total sampling error is plus or minus 3.4 percent.
